newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila denies row with Yankee bond underwriters.
newsitem.headline: Manila denies row with Yankee bond underwriters.

text.p: The Philippine Central Bank on Friday denied market rumours its inaugural Yankee bond issue was bogged down by infighting among members of its underwriting syndicate and said it was now the ideal time for a launch.

"It is an opportune time for BSP (Central Bank) to relaunch the bond," the bank said in a statement, hours after Bank governor Gabriel Singson announced that it would rebid the underwriting services to a single investment house on a firm basis.
Rumours of infighting among syndicate members on the timing and pricing of the issue had swept the market forcing the Central Bank to call a crucial meeting on Thursday to change the offering tack.
However, Singson and syndicate members denied the rumours.
The syndicate was led by Salomon Brothers, with JP Morgan, Citicorp, Merrill Lynch, Morgan Stanley and ING Barings as the co-arrangers.

"Central Bank has maintained good working relationship with Salomon Brothers over the past months ... If we're unhappy with Salomon, why did we invite them to the bidding?" Singson told Reuters earlier.
An official of one of the co-arrangers said relations among the members were cordial, and the change in the underwriting structure was due to a change in market conditions.
He said it would not affect the offering itself.
"(The change) is not common, but it's not unusual ... The offering should be judged by its result rather than by its approach," he said.
Last April, the launch of country's first sovereign Yankee bond was marred by a last-minute decision to postpone it due to rising U.S. interest rates.
The Central Bank was willing to pay up to 205 basis points above the prevailing Treasury bond rate, but was told investors were looking at a 230 basis point spread.
In February, the Monetary Board was only looking at a spread of about 150 to 160 basis points when it agreed to tap the U.S. market, Singson said.
"The current U.S. market situation has significantly improved over the past periods ... However, this period may not last very long," the Central Bank statement said.
Singson said the rebidding would be done soon with all the members of the original syndicate participating.

Under the new structure, the winning underwriter would pay the Central Bank the entire proceeds before it sells the bond to the market. Under the original contract, the underwriting syndicate was meant to sell the bonds only on a best effort basis.
Singson said the bank was willing to lower its offering size to less than $750 million to be able to achieve better pricing.
Salomon Brothers and the five co-arrangers have agreed to the new bidding rule. Singson declined to give specifics, and the syndicate members were also told to keep the rules confidential.
Salomon Brothers said it had accepted the revision of the underwriting contract and was ready to join the rebidding.

"Salomon Brothers intends to participate. Based on our conversations with BSP, we can confirm that the need for a second bidding process has absolutely nothing to do with the perceived quality of Salomon Borthers' advice or service," Katherin D'arcy, Salomon's corporate communications chief in Hong Kong, said.
